claims.text: Conventional strengthening approaches typically improve strength at the expense of ductility.
A conventionally processed low-alloy steel or aluminum alloy typically has a uniform grain structure.
Severe plastic deformation induces high strain and grain refinement.
Controlled annealing after severe plastic deformation can produce a spatially graded or hierarchical grain-size distribution.
The resulting microstructure will contain ultrafine-grained regions coexisting with relatively coarse-grained regions.
Grain refinement increases strength through grain-boundary strengthening.
Coarse-grained regions accommodate plastic deformation and promote strain partitioning.
Strain accommodation in the more deformable regions mitigates local stress concentration.
Mitigating local stress concentration improves ductility by reducing crack formation.
Combining ultrafine and coarse grains can overcome the strength-ductility trade-off found in uniformly processed metals.
Severe plastic deformation followed by controlled annealing will increase yield strength relative to a uniformly grain-sized control.
Severe plastic deformation followed by controlled annealing will improve ductility relative to a uniformly grain-sized control.
The improvements in both yield strength and ductility will be statistically significant.
The proposed approach applies broadly to structural metals without adding alloying elements.
Changes in deformation severity and annealing parameters will alter the gradient microstructure and resulting mechanical properties.
Testing is proposed under ambient-temperature, quasi-static loading.

contradictions.description: The intervention requires a controlled annealing treatment, which ordinarily entails elevated temperature, while the boundary states that the structural metals are processed at ambient temperature. The conditions field may intend ambient-temperature testing, but the boundary explicitly applies ambient temperature to processing.
